'''Gloria C. Gilmer''' ({{née}} '''Ford'''; June 28, 1928 – August 25, 2021) was an American mathematician and educator, notable for being the first African American woman to publish a non-PhD thesis.

== Early life and education ==
Gilmer was born in [[Baltimore]], Maryland on June 28, 1928. She studied for her [[Bachelor of Science]] degree at [[Morgan State University]],<ref name=BioWomen>{{cite web|title=Gloria Ford Gilmer|url=http://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/gilmer.htm|publisher=Agnes Scott College|accessdate=June 1, 2014|last=Riddle|first=Larry|website=Biographies of Women Mathematicians}}</ref><ref name=BlackWomenAmerica>{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/blackwomeninamer00hine/|chapter=Gilmer, Gloria|last=Kenschaft|first=Patricia Clark|title=Black Women in America: An Historical Encyclopedia|editor-last1=Hine|editor-first1=Darlene Clark|editor-last2=Brown|editor-first2=Elsa Barkley|editor-last3=Terborg-Penn|editor-first3=Rosalyn|year=1993|publisher=Carlson Publishing|location=Brooklyn, New York|isbn=978-0-926019-61-4|access-date=10 June 2020}}</ref> where she was part of the class of 1949.<ref name="Morgan Magazine">{{cite news|last1=Addison|first1=Eric|title=Giving back by the numbers: Gloria Ford Gilmer, Ph.D., '49|url=https://issuu.com/morganstateu/docs/mag_vol_i_2011_v0.2.5r__to_web|accessdate=9 April 2017|work=Morgan Magazine|issue=1|publisher=Morgan State University|date=October 27, 2011|page=16}}</ref>  While there, she published two papers with her supervisor [[Luna Mishoe]];<ref name=MAA>{{cite web|url=https://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/pdf/centennial/African_Americans.pdf|title=African-American Mathematicians and the Mathematical Association of America|date=2015|last1=Nkwanta|first1=Asamoah|last2=Barber|first2=Janet E.|access-date=10 June 2020|archive-date=28 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200928030332/https://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/pdf/centennial/African_Americans.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mishoe|first1=Luna I.|last2=Ford|first2=Gloria C.|date=1956-02-01|title=On the limit of the coefficients of the eigenfunction series associated with a certain non-self-adjoint differential system|url=https://www.ams.org/jourcgi/jour-getitem?pii=S0002-9939-1956-0077754-3|journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society|language=en|volume=7|issue=2|pages=260|doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1956-0077754-3|issn=0002-9939|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mishoe|first1=L.I.|last2=Ford|first2=G.C.|date=1956|title=On the uniform convergence of a certain eigenfunction series.|url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.pjm/1103044127|journal=Pacific Journal of Mathematics|language=en|volume=6|issue=2|pages=271–278|doi=10.2140/pjm.1956.6.271|issn=0030-8730|doi-access=free}}</ref> these were the first two research papers published by an African American woman, being published in 1956,<ref name=AAMII>{{cite conference|conference=African Americans in Mathematics II: Fourth Conference for African-American Researchers in the Mathematical Sciences, June 16–19, 1998, Rice University, Houston, Texas|title=Black Research Mathematicians in the United States|last=Williams|first=Scott W.|series=Contemporary Mathematics|volume=252|year=1999|pages=165–168|doi=10.1090/conm/252/13|publisher=American Mathematical Society|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=MDC>{{cite journal|journal=Polygon|publisher=[[Miami Dade College]]|url=https://issuu.com/mdc-polygon/docs/polygon2010|access-date=10 June 2020|title=African Americans in Mathematical Sciences – A Chronological Introduction|last=Shakil|first=M.|date=21 April 2015|pages=27–42|archive-date=15 March 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220315115236/https://issuu.com/mdc-polygon/docs/polygon2010|url-status=dead}}</ref> under her maiden name of Gloria C. Ford. She was also a student of [[Clarence Stephens]] while there.<ref name=Buffalo>{{cite web|url = http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/PEEPS/gilmer_gloria.html|title=Gloria Ford Gilmer|website=Black Women in Mathematics|publisher=State University of New York at Buffalo|last=Williams|first=Scott W.|year=2008|access-date=10 June 2020}}</ref><ref name="Morgan Magazine"/>

After receiving her [[Master of Arts|MA]] in Mathematics at the [[University of Pennsylvania]],<ref name=BioWomen/> she went to work on ballistics research at the [[Aberdeen Proving Ground]],<ref name="Morgan Magazine"/> and later to teach at six [[HBCUs]].<ref name=Buffalo/>  She studied for a PhD at the [[University of Wisconsin-Madison]], but left after a year, later citing "a marriage, children, and the necessity to earn a living".<ref name=Buffalo/>  Between 1965 and 1966, Gilmer became the first African American mathematics instructor at the Milwaukee Area Technical College  and the first Black woman to teach mathematics at the [[University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Moore |first1=Tanya |last2=Levy |first2=Josh |date=2024-03-01 |title=The Unfailing Optimism of Dr. Gloria Ford Gilmer (1928–2021) |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/202403/rnoti-p366.pdf |journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=71 |issue=3 |pages=1 |doi=10.1090/noti2895  |doi-access=free|issn=0002-9920}}</ref> She subsequently gained a PhD from [[Marquette University]],<ref name=BlackWomenAmerica/> in Education Administration.<ref name=Buffalo/> The title of her dissertation is "Effects Of Small Discussion Groups On Self-Paced Instruction In a Developmental Algebra Course".<ref>{{Cite web|title=Gloria Gilmer Abstract|url=https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/abstracts/gilmer_abstract.htm|access-date=2020-06-10|website=www.agnesscott.edu}}</ref>

== Post-doctoral career ==
[[File:Photo of Gloria Ford Gilmer in 1948 Morgan State College Yearbook.png|thumb|Gilmer in 1948]]
Much of Gilmer's work has been in [[ethnomathematics]]; she was described as a "leader in the field" by [[Scott W. Williams]], a mathematics professor at [[SUNY Buffalo]].<ref name="Buffalo" />

An example of this research is when, based on fieldwork in New York and Baltimore, Gilmer and her assistants, 14-year-old Stephanie Desgrottes and teacher Mary Potter, observed and interviewed both hair stylists and customers in the two cities' salons, inquiring about [[tessellations]] in [[box braids]] (box-shaped tessellations resembling brick walls) and triangular braids (tessellations resembling equilateral triangles), two styles that restrict the movement of the hair when the head is tossed. While these hair stylists do not generally think of what they do as mathematical, Gilmer detailed the many mathematically based patterns in these and other types of braiding and how they are found in nature, such as the tessellating hexagons found in braids that resembles the flesh of pineapples and the honeycombs in beehives. As an educator, Gilmer used these results to create classroom activities for students to understand the mathematics of hair braiding.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|title=Mathematical Patterns in African American Hairstyles|url=http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/special/gilmer-gloria_HAIRSTYLES.html|last=Gilmer|first=Gloria|year=2008|access-date=10 June 2020|website=Mathematicians of the African Diaspora}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Bangura|first=Abdul Karim|title=African Mathematics: From Bones to Computers|publisher=University Press of America|year=2011|isbn=978-0-7618-5348-0}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Ethnomathematics: An African American Perspective On Developing Women In Mathematics|url=https://www.nottingham.ac.uk/csme/meas/papers/gilmer.html|access-date=2020-06-10|website=www.nottingham.ac.uk|archive-date=2021-07-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210725221646/https://www.nottingham.ac.uk/csme/meas/papers/gilmer.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In the early 1980s, Gilmer was the first African American woman to be on the board of governors of the Mathematical Association of America.<ref name=BlackWomenAmerica/> Between 1981 and 1984, Gilmer was a research associate at the [[United States Department of Education]], where she was part of the Office of Educational Research and Improvement.<ref name=BioWomen/> Gilmer traveled to Adelaide, Australia in 1984 to attend the Fifth [[International Commission on Mathematical Instruction|International Commission of Mathematical Education]] (ICME-5) to present on improvements to the IEA Mathematics Study, an international mathematics assessment test.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Moore |first1=Tanya |last2=Levy |first2=Josh |date=2024-03-01 |title=The Unfailing Optimism of Dr. Gloria Ford Gilmer (1928–2021) |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/202403/rnoti-p366.pdf |journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=71 |issue=3 |pages=1 |doi=10.1090/noti2895  |doi-access=free|issn=0002-9920}}</ref> In 1985 she co-founded and the executive board of International Study Group on Ethnomathematics (ISGEm),<ref>{{cite web|website=ISGEm International Study Group on Ethnomathematics|title=Main Page|url=http://isgem.rpi.edu/|access-date=10 June 2020|archive-date=28 March 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150328104801/http://isgem.rpi.edu/|url-status=dead}}</ref> of which she was the President from 1985 to 1996.<ref name=BioWomen/>  She was also the second person, and first woman, to give the [[National Association of Mathematicians]]' Cox-Talbot lecture, which was named in honour of the first and fourth African Americans to receive PhDs in mathematics.<ref name=CoxTalbot>{{cite web|url=https://www.nam-math.org/cox-talbot-lecture.html|title=Cox-Talbot Lecture|website=National Association of Mathematicians|access-date=10 June 2020|archive-date=14 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210214165933/https://www.nam-math.org/cox-talbot-lecture.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2008, Gilmer became the president of Math-Tech, a corporation that aims to take new research material and create more effective mathematics curricula, particularly with respect to women and minorities.<ref name=Buffalo/><ref name=":0" />

In 2022, Gilmer became the first Black woman mathematician to have her papers archived in the Manuscript Division of the Library of Congress.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Milwaukeean becomes first Black woman mathematician to have her papers in Library of Congress manuscript collection |url=https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2023/01/10/library-of-congress-collects-papers-of-milwaukee-mathematician/69775125007/ |access-date=2023-02-21 |website=Journal Sentinel |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Death ==
Gilmer died on August 25, 2021, at the age of 93, in the city of [[Milwaukee]], in the state of [[Wisconsin]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Milwaukee mathematician, teacher inspired Black students to see math within themselves|url=https://www.jsonline.com/story/news/education/2021/10/01/milwaukee-mathematician-remembered-wisconsins-hidden-figure/5834699001/|access-date=2022-01-15|website=Milwaukee Journal Sentinel|language=en}}</ref><ref name="Morgan Magazine"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Mrs. Gloria Ford Gilmer |url=https://www.northwestfuneralchapel.com/obituaries/Gloria-Gilmer/#!/Obituary |website=Northwest Funeral Chapel |access-date=15 November 2023}}</ref>

== List of published works ==
{{Expand list|date=June 2020}}
* "On the Limit of the Coefficients of the Eigenfunction Series Associated with a Certain Non-self-adjoint Differential System," with Luna I. Mishoe. Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society 7.2 (1956): 260.
* "On the Uniform Convergence of a Certain Eigenfunction Series," with Luna Mishoe. Pacific Journal of Mathematics 6.2 (1956): 271–78.
* "Effects Of Small Discussion Groups On Self-Paced Instruction In a Developmental Algebra Course" (1978). Dissertations (1962-2010) Access via Proquest Digital Dissertations. AAI7905173. <nowiki>https://epublications.marquette.edu/dissertations/AAI7905173</nowiki>
* "Mathematical Patterns in African American Hairstyles." Presented at the 77th Annual Meeting of the National Council of Teachers in Mathematics (1998).
* "Ethnomathematics: An African American Perspective On Developing Women In Mathematics."  In ''Changing the Faces of Mathematics: Perspectives on Gender.''  National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (2001). ({{ISBN|978-0-87353-496-3}})

== Awards ==
The [[American Mathematical Society]] (AMS) has a mid-career research fellowship, the Claytor-Gilmer Fellowship, named after Gilmer and [[William Schieffelin Claytor]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=The AMS Claytor-Gilmer Fellowship|url=https://www.ams.org/programs/ams-fellowships/claytor-gilmer|access-date=2021-05-24|website=American Mathematical Society|language=en}}</ref>
